Fringe
FRINJ
noun
From the Old French frenge, from Late Latin fimbria, “a border or fringe.” In the KJV it renders the Hebrew tzitzit, the twisted tassel commanded on the corners of the garment — not a decorative edge but a memorial appointed by God.

Biblical Definition

A fringe in the Authorized Version is the tassel — the tzitzit — that the LORD commanded Israel to wear on the corners of the garment as a standing memorial of His commandments. It is not, as the modern ear supposes, a mere ornamental border or a decorative trim; it is a preaching thread, appointed to catch the eye and turn the heart. The LORD is exact about both its making and its meaning. “Bid them that they make them fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue” (Num 15:38). The blue thread lifted the eye heavenward. And the purpose follows plainly: “that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them; and that ye seek not after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go a whoring” (Num 15:39). The tassel was an outward help against an inward wandering — a thing seen, set against the roving of the heart and the eyes. Moses repeats the charge in Deuteronomy: “Thou shalt make thee fringes upon the four quarters of thy vesture” (Deu 22:12). So the godly Israelite carried the Law woven at his hem, that a glance downward might recall him from sin to obedience. The fringe preached; the question was always whether the wearer would remember, or merely be seen wearing it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The commanded tassel on the corners of the Israelite’s garment, worn as a memorial of God’s law.

FRINGE, an ornamental border of threads or tassels; in Scripture, the appointed tassel on the garment’s corners.

From Late Latin fimbria, a border or fringe, through Old French frenge.

The KJV uses it of the tzitzit, commanded with a ribband of blue as a memorial.

Israel was to make fringes in the borders of their garments (Num 15:38).

Its purpose was to make them remember and do the commandments of the LORD (Num 15:39).

Key Scripture

Num 15:38 — "Speak unto the children of Israel, and bid them that they make them fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue:"

Num 15:39 — "And it shall be unto you for a fringe, that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them; and that ye seek not after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go a whoring:"

Deu 22:12 — "Thou shalt make thee fringes upon the four quarters of thy vesture, wherewith thou coverest thyself."

Num 15:40 — "That ye may remember, and do all my commandments, and be holy unto your God."

Modern Corruption

The modern ear hears “fringe” as a decorative trim or the far edge of a thing; the AV means a God-commanded memorial tassel.

expand to see more

The honest drift has carried the word two ways, both misleading. To the modern ear a fringe is either a bit of decorative trim on a curtain or lampshade, or else the outer margin of a thing — the “fringe” of a crowd, the “lunatic fringe” of a movement. Neither catches what the LORD commanded. The biblical fringe was not ornament and not margin; it was a memorial, a divinely appointed tassel with a thread of blue, meant to be looked at and obeyed. It sat at the edge of the garment, but it stood at the center of a duty: to remember the commandments and do them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that softening into mere decoration. The principle to recover is God’s kindness in giving His people outward helps against inward drift. The fringe was a mercy to weak memories: a thing seen, set against “your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go a whoring” (Num 15:39). The LORD knew the roving eye and the wandering heart, and appointed a visible sign to recall His people to obedience. Under the new covenant the tassel is gone, but the principle abides in the ordinances Christ has given His church — the Word read and preached, the water, the bread and cup — outward and visible helps that catch the eye and turn the heart to remember. The danger, then as now, was to wear the sign and forget the substance, to keep the tassel and lose the LORD; but rightly used, the fringe preached obedience at every glance.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means the commanded tassel on the garment’s corners — a memorial of the law, not a decorative trim.

expand to see more

Fringe — from Late Latin fimbria, “a border or fringe.”

In the KJV it renders the Hebrew tzitzit, the appointed tassel.

It bore a ribband of blue to lift the eye toward heaven (Num 15:38).

Its purpose was remembrance and obedience of the commandments (Num 15:39).

Israel wore fringes on the four quarters of the garment (Deu 22:12).

Usage

"The KJV’s fringe is a commanded memorial tassel, not the decorative edge of a rug."

"The fringe bore a thread of blue, that a glance might recall the commandments of the LORD."

"He was to seek not after his own heart, but to look upon the fringe and remember."
